title: How to Spot a Real Vintage Tee (And Skip the Reprints)
description: Seams, cracking, cut and tag — four checks that tell you in ten seconds whether you're holding a genuine nineties tee or last year's reprint.
excerpt: Reprints look identical in a listing photo. In your hands they don't. Here's what to look for.
content:
Vintage tees got expensive, and expensive pulls in reprints. In a marketplace photo they look identical to the real thing. In your hands they don't — and you can tell in about ten seconds once you know where to look.

## Start under the arms

This is the fastest test. Tees from the eighties and earlier have single-stitch hems — one row of stitching — and, more importantly, no side seams at all, because the body was knitted as a tube. Double stitching and side seams came in around the mid-nineties. If someone is selling you a 1987 tour tee with side seams and a double-stitched hem, you're buying a reprint.

## The print has to crack correctly

Old screen prints wear from the inside out. The ink splits along fine lines exactly where the fabric folds most — chest, shoulders, hem. Fake distressing is applied flat, so the cracking is even across the whole graphic, including places the shirt never bends. Rub the print between your fingers too: a real one is thin and sits in the cotton, a new one feels rubbery and sits on top of it.

## Cut and tag

Decades of washing shrink a shirt vertically, so genuinely old tees run shorter and boxier. If the proportions match a shirt you'd buy on the high street today, something is off. The tag closes the case: a crossed-out size, single-colour printing and missing modern wash symbols usually point to an older piece.

## The takeaway

Seams, cracking, cut, tag. Four checks, one minute, and you stop paying vintage prices for last year's stock. For streetwear that's already been curated for you, browse [DOPESTORE](https://dopestore.cz) — and if you film your finds, [TubeVoice](https://tubevoice.io) dubs the videos into dozens of languages.
